newsitem.title: USA: Democrats vow to block Senate over disaster aid.
newsitem.headline: Democrats vow to block Senate over disaster aid.

text.p: Senate Democrats threatened Friday to hold up work until disaster relief for flood-stricken states is assured and President Clinton again vowed to veto the version pressed by Republicans.

Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle called callous the Republican decision to delay sending the disaster relief bill to the White House until next week. It passed Thursday with two provisions Clinton has refused to accept.
In a written statement, Clinton urged Congress to send him a straightforward disaster relief bill without legislative riders added by Republicans.
"I have no choice but to veto that measure," he said.
"Unfortunately, the Republican leaders of Congress have chosen the path of partisanship and confrontation in their actions on the disaster relief bill," Clinton added.
Daschle, a South Dakota Democrat, told reporters, "We will not allow legislation to move in Congress until this issue is resolved."
His state was one of 35 in need of federal assistance for recovery from weather damage. South Dakota and much of the upper plains were still reeling from floods of monumental proportions.

North Dakota Democratic Sen. Byron Dorgan said the unrelated measures were added by Republicans to the emergency spending bill in an effort to force the president to sign into law measures he would normally have refused.

The bill provides $5.4 billion for disaster assistance, including $89 million for House Speaker Newt Gingrich's home state of Georgia and $24 million for Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott's state of Mississippi.

Rebutting Republican claims that there is money in the federal pipeline to provide emergency relief, Daschle insisted there were no funds available to begin permanent recovery. Money is needed by farmers to start rebuilding herds, by homeowners who await buyouts of homes in flood plains and by businesses to rebuild their inventories, he said.

The bill also contained $1.9 billion to pay for military operations in Bosnia and the Gulf and $262 million for feeding poor women and their children, for education and for a new transportation system at Yosemite National Park.

Republican leaders of both the House and Senate refused to remove two provisions Clinton has said he will not accept -- the first to avert another government shutdown over the federal budget and the second to block the use of sampling to include uncounted minorities in the 2000 census.
A spokeswoman for Gingrich said they were operating on the assumption the president would sign the bill into law as he has pledged to send disaster relief to the states.

Thursday, Lott said he will call the president's bluff on the disaster assistance and assumed the president will sign the bill despite repeated insistance by Clinton himself and his aides that it will be vetoed.
